name: Boswellia serrata

lead: Boswellia is a resin extract taken to ease joint pain and speed recovery, so people can train more often and with less aching toward a more muscular physique.

Its boswellic acids, especially AKBA, inhibit 5-lipoxygenase and reduce leukotriene production, which lowers inflammatory signaling. Meta-analyses of knee osteoarthritis trials report improvements in pain, stiffness and function. Those trials looked at osteoarthritis, not training outcomes, and many were small and industry-linked.

paras: Taken as a standardized extract capsule, commonly daily and often combined with curcumin, glucosamine or fish oil. Users typically report joint changes after a few weeks. It has a long history in Ayurvedic medicine.

Side effects are generally mild, such as stomach upset or diarrhea. Product standardization varies, and safety in pregnancy has not been established. Legal as a dietary supplement; over-harvesting of wild trees is an ecological concern.

angle.text: Boswellia is taken to ease joint pain and speed recovery, so users can train harder and more often in pursuit of more muscle and a leaner look. Trials have studied osteoarthritis pain rather than training outcomes.

lead: Boswellia serrata is a tree native to India and neighbouring parts of the Indian subcontinent whose gum resin, known as Indian frankincense, has long been used in Ayurvedic medicine [1][2]. The resin contains pentacyclic triterpenoids called boswellic acids, including beta-boswellic acid and acetyl-11-keto-beta-boswellic acid (AKBA), which are the compounds most often used to standardise commercial extracts [1][3].

Extracts are sold as dietary supplements for joint comfort and general inflammation, frequently combined with curcumin, glucosamine, bromelain or fish oil. The best-studied use is knee osteoarthritis, where small randomised trials and meta-analyses report improvements in pain, stiffness and function over placebo [4][5]. It has no established direct role in facial or body aesthetics; in appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a recovery and joint-comfort supplement for people who train.

Reviews describe the clinical literature as promising but limited by small sample sizes, short durations and frequent industry involvement in trials of branded extracts [6][4]. Reported adverse effects are generally minor, such as gastrointestinal upset [7].
infobox: Sold as a supplement in many countries

paras: Boswellia serrata is a deciduous tree of dry forests in India and surrounding regions. Its resin is collected by making incisions in the bark [2]. The genus Boswellia contains other frankincense-producing species, such as Boswellia carterii, which are sometimes grouped together in reviews of frankincense's therapeutic properties [3].
Wikipedia notes that the species is under pressure from unsustainable harvesting practices, which is a recurring conservation concern attached to the commercial resin trade [1].

No published trial has tested oral Boswellia serrata for facial appearance, body composition or other aesthetic outcomes. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities it appears mainly as an ingredient in joint and anti-inflammatory stacks aimed at keeping training comfortable [8].

Traditional Ayurvedic use centres on inflammatory conditions such as arthritis, as well as respiratory and digestive complaints [2]. Modern research has focused on osteoarthritis, with smaller bodies of work on inflammatory bowel disease, radiation-related brain swelling and other conditions [4][9][10]. A topical over-the-counter pain patch containing Boswellia serrata alongside other botanicals is listed in the US DailyMed database for temporary relief of minor muscle and joint aches [11].

Laboratory work from the early 1990s reported that boswellic acids inhibit 5-lipoxygenase, the enzyme that produces leukotrienes, with acetyl-11-keto-beta-boswellic acid the most potent in rat neutrophil experiments [12]. A related in vitro study compared boswellic acids with curcumin and described distinct anti-inflammatory mechanisms for each [13]. Later cell studies reported effects on NF-kappa B signalling [14].
Reviews also describe inhibition of leukocyte elastase and effects on inflammatory cytokines, but note that much of the mechanistic data come from cell and animal models [3][15].

Boswellic acids are poorly water soluble and have been described as having low oral bioavailability, which has motivated branded extracts marketed as having enhanced absorption, including formulations that combine AKBA with other boswellic acids [16][5][15]. Product composition varies between manufacturers and standardisation is not uniform.

Osteoarthritis is the main condition studied. A 2020 meta-analysis of seven randomised trials with 545 participants reported that Boswellia and its extracts reduced pain (VAS and WOMAC pain), stiffness and functional limitation compared with controls, and concluded they may be an effective and safe option, while the authors of such pooled analyses acknowledge small trial sizes [4]. A 2018 network meta-analysis of dietary supplements for osteoarthritis placed Boswellia serrata extract among seven supplements with large short-term pain effects, though it cautioned about trial quality and that clinically important effects were rarely sustained at medium term across supplements [6].

Individual randomised, placebo-controlled trials of branded extracts have reported symptom improvements. These include a 30-day trial of 70 knee osteoarthritis patients using an enhanced-bioavailability extract that also measured inflammatory and cartilage biomarkers [5], a pilot trial of 48 patients with a combined AKBA and beta-boswellic acid extract [16], and a 2003 crossover trial in 30 patients [17]. More recent trials have examined Boswellia combined with celery (Apium graveolens) extract [8], an extract assessed for cartilage morphology on imaging [18], and Boswellia with or without an omega-3 product in people over 40 with persistent knee pain [19]. Several of these studies were supported by the manufacturers of the extracts tested.

Outside joint disease, a small randomised pilot trial in patients irradiated for brain tumours examined cerebral oedema [9], and a later report examined cerebral radiation necrosis after radiosurgery [10]. A 2001 trial of the gum resin in chronic colitis was also published [20]. Registered trials listed on ClinicalTrials.gov include studies of topical Boswellia for radiation dermatitis, oral extract in acute diarrhoea, and combinations with curcumin or bromelain after COVID-19 or breast surgery; most are small and several have not reported results [21][22][23][24].

An overview of systematic reviews of herbal medicines classified the adverse effects of Boswellia serrata as minor [7]. Commonly reported effects in trials and reviews are gastrointestinal, such as stomach upset or diarrhoea [15]. Safety in pregnancy and breastfeeding has not been established, and the topical product label advises pregnant or breastfeeding users to consult a health professional [11].
Reviews of pharmacokinetic and clinical data note that long-term safety data are limited and that interactions with prescription drugs have been little studied [15].

subs.h: Use in looksmaxxing and training communities
paras: On the T Nation bodybuilding forum, users have described taking Boswellia daily for arthritic knees and joint mobility [25], asked whether it helps chronic toe-joint pain [26], and listed it among inflammation-modulating supplements alongside quercetin, pine bark extract and fish oil [27][28]. It also appears as a minor ingredient in multi-component recovery products discussed on the same forum [29][30]. Discussion in these communities is generally anecdotal and focused on joint comfort rather than appearance.
Boswellia serrata extracts are sold as dietary supplements in many jurisdictions. Concern about over-harvesting of wild trees accompanies the growth of the supplement market [1].

Ongoing registered studies include a trial of Boswellia on pain sensitisation in healthy volunteers, planned trials in radiotherapy toxicity for prostate and head-and-neck cancers, and earlier window-of-opportunity work in breast cancer [31][32][21][33]. Laboratory studies of AKBA have examined effects on angiogenesis and tumour growth in animal models of prostate cancer; these have not been established in human treatment [34].

lore.intro: Boswellia is discussed in training and joint-health forums mainly as a natural anti-inflammatory for sore joints, often as one part of a multi-ingredient stack [25][28].
